standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Parental wellbeing & mental health; burnout; your own needs matter; the Life-Skills Toolkit under load (UNESCO 5.6, 5.5). New v2 build, the parent's-own-wellbeing node and a high-care one: you can't pour from an empty cup. Six modes: the empty cup (spot burnout and bust 'good parents sacrifice everything'; self-care is part of childcare, not selfish, and struggling is not failing), your needs count (protect your needs, identity and a little time of your own without guilt; you're still a whole person), baby blues and beyond (normalise the common, passing baby blues and recognise postpartum depression and anxiety, in yourself or a partner and in fathers too, with frightening intrusive thoughts treated as a symptom and a cue to get help, never a verdict), reach out (help-seeking is strength not weakness, build a support net, and you needn't be in crisis to deserve help), healthy coping (safe strategies under load, rest, breathe, move, connect, accept help, with unhealthy coping gently swapped out; never any pain or discomfort technique), tools & help (a breathing space, a help-finder and crisis routing). High-care and non-shaming: any sign of postnatal depression or anxiety, or any crisis, is met with warmth and an immediate route to help, concern plus resources; healthy coping only and explicitly not therapy, always signposting professional care; includes fathers and addresses joint-family pressure and stigma. Builds on Mind & Belonging (g49) and Bounce (g39); protects the parent so they can do everything else in Chapter 8. India: postpartum depression affects around one in five (about 22%) Indian mothers, nearly double the global average and badly under-recognised amid heavy expectations and stigma; fathers can be affected too (around one in ten); routes to Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN 1800-599-0019, a doctor, and emergency 112.

evidenceBase: Parental wellbeing is part of childcare, not a luxury: you cannot pour from an empty cup, parental burnout (ongoing exhaustion, detachment and feeling overwhelmed) is real and a signal to rest and seek support rather than push harder, and struggling is not failing. Each parent remains a whole person whose needs, identity and a little time of their own still matter and make them a steadier parent, so protecting them is non-selfish, good parenting; the framing is warm and explicitly non-shaming and includes fathers as well as mothers (WHO parental and maternal mental health; parental-burnout research; UNESCO life-skills and wellbeing)

Postpartum mental health is common, real and treatable, and it must be recognised rather than hidden: mild 'baby blues', tearfulness and mood swings in the first days, are very common and usually pass within about two weeks, whereas postpartum depression and anxiety, lasting low, anxious or numb feelings, loss of interest in the baby or oneself, are medical conditions that need care and affect around one in five (about 22%) of Indian mothers, nearly double the global average, with fathers affected too at around one in ten. Frightening intrusive thoughts can accompany postnatal anxiety and are a symptom and a cue to get help quickly, never a verdict on the person, and partners should watch out for and support each other (WHO maternal mental health; India postpartum-depression prevalence and paternal postnatal-depression research)

Help-seeking is a strength and healthy coping is learnable, and this node supports and signposts but is not therapy: reaching out early, before crisis, to trusted people, a doctor or a helpline genuinely turns things around, and a support network is how humans are meant to raise children rather than in isolation. Healthy coping under load means rest, breathing, gentle movement, connection and accepting help, with unhealthy coping gently swapped out and never any strategy involving pain or discomfort, and any sign of postnatal depression or anxiety or any crisis is met with warmth and an immediate route to help, Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN 1800-599-0019, a doctor, and emergency 112 for immediate danger, with care always pointed to professionals (Tele-MANAS / KIRAN; perinatal mental-health and help-seeking guidance)

scenarios.hook: "A good parent sacrifices everything and needs nothing for themselves."
scenarios.relearn: Self-care is part of childcare, not selfishness; an empty cup pours nothing.

myth.un: A good parent sacrifices everything and needs nothing for themselves.
myth.re: You can't pour from an empty cup; looking after yourself is part of looking after your child, not selfish.
myth.why: A depleted parent has less to give.

scenarios.hook: "Burnout is just normal tiredness you should push through."
scenarios.relearn: Parental burnout is real and a signal to rest and get support, not just tiredness to push through.

myth.un: Burnout is just normal tiredness you should push through.
myth.re: Parental burnout is real, ongoing exhaustion, detachment and feeling overwhelmed, and it's a signal to rest and get support, not push harder.
myth.why: Burnout is a signal, not a weakness.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign of parental burnout to take seriously, or ordinary busy-day tiredness?
scenarios.relearn: Constant drain, detachment and dread are burnout signals; a single rough night or post-outing tiredness is ordinary.

items.text: Dreading each day, nothing left to give
Being tired after a long outing

scenarios.hook: You're running on empty but feel guilty even thinking about your own needs.
scenarios.relearn: Refuel yourself as part of caring for your child; self-depletion isn't devotion.

options.text: Treat refuelling yourself as part of caring for your child
options.consequence: You give from a fuller, steadier place.

options.text: Keep draining yourself to prove devotion
options.consequence: Refuelling lets you care from a fuller place; draining yourself to prove devotion leaves less for your child, not more.

scenarios.debrief: Caring for yourself refuels your capacity to parent; depleting yourself helps no one.

scenarios.hook: Match each sign to what it's telling you.
scenarios.relearn: Exhaustion, short temper and numbness are signals to rest, refill and reach for help, not to push harder.

pairs.right: You're burning out, rest and get support
Your reserves are empty, refill them

pairs.left: Feeling numb to things you loved
pairs.right: A signal to reach for help

scenarios.hook: Sam: looking after yourself isn't taking away from your child; it's part of what you give them. Sit right?
scenarios.relearn: Looking after yourself is part of what you give your child, not something taken from them.
scenarios.affirm: Self-care isn't taken from your child; a steadier, refuelled parent is part of what you give them.

scenarios.hook: Spot the healthy response to running on empty.
scenarios.relearn: Meet burnout by resting, accepting help and reaching out, not by pushing to collapse.

scene.text: Resting and accepting help when you can
Pushing harder until you collapse
Naming the burnout and reaching out

scenarios.why: Resting, accepting help and reaching out are healthy; pushing to collapse harms you and the family.

scenarios.hook: "If I admit I'm struggling as a parent, I'm failing."
scenarios.relearn: Admitting you're struggling isn't failing; it's the brave first step toward getting the support you need.

myth.un: If I admit I'm struggling as a parent, I'm failing.
myth.re: Struggling is not failing; parenting is genuinely hard, and naming the struggle is the brave first step to coping.

scenarios.hook: You haven't had a moment to yourself in so long you've stopped noticing how depleted you are.
scenarios.relearn: Build tiny regular refills in now; a depleted parent can't wait for a someday free day.

options.text: Build in small, regular refills, even ten minutes, as a non-negotiable
options.consequence: You stop the slow slide into burnout.

options.text: Wait for a free day that never comes
options.consequence: Small regular refills prevent the slide into burnout; waiting for a free day means never refilling at all.

scenarios.debrief: Protect small, regular refills for yourself; don't wait for a free day that never arrives.

scenarios.hook: Sam: even the most devoted parent has limits, and respecting yours keeps you in the game. Land okay?
scenarios.relearn: Even the most devoted parent has limits; respecting yours keeps you going.
scenarios.affirm: Every parent has limits; respecting yours, rather than overriding them, is what keeps you going for your child.

scenarios.hook: Sort: protects a parent from burnout, or speeds it up?
scenarios.relearn: Accepting help and small rests protect you; doing it all alone and feeling guilty for breaks speed burnout.

items.text: Accepting help and sharing the load

scenarios.hook: A fellow parent confides they're completely burnt out and ashamed of it.
scenarios.relearn: Support a burnt-out parent with warmth and help, not 'everyone copes, toughen up'.

options.text: Tell them it's common, not shameful, and help them find support
options.consequence: They feel less alone and more able to act.

options.text: Tell them everyone copes and to toughen up
options.consequence: Naming burnout as common and helping them find support eases the shame; 'toughen up' deepens the isolation.

scenarios.debrief: Meet a burnt-out parent with 'it's common, not shameful' and help finding support, never 'toughen up'.

scenarios.hook: "Once you're a parent, your own needs and identity stop mattering."
scenarios.relearn: Your needs and identity still matter as a parent; keeping them alive makes you steadier, not selfish.

myth.un: Once you're a parent, your own needs and identity stop mattering.
myth.re: You're still a whole person with real needs and an identity; keeping them alive makes you a steadier parent.
myth.why: A self is the ground you parent from.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a legitimate parent's need, or a 'selfish' want to feel guilty about?
scenarios.relearn: Rest, a little time, connection and a thing you love are all legitimate needs, none worth guilt.

scenarios.hook: "Taking any time for yourself makes you a bad, selfish parent."
scenarios.relearn: Taking a little time for yourself isn't selfish; it refills you and models self-respect for your child.

myth.un: Taking any time for yourself makes you a bad, selfish parent.
myth.re: A little time for yourself refills you and models healthy self-respect for your child; it's good parenting.

scenarios.hook: You feel like you've vanished into 'just a parent' and miss who you were.
scenarios.relearn: Reclaim bits of who you are; you needn't accept that parenthood erased you for good.

options.text: Reclaim small pieces of your own identity, bit by bit
options.consequence: You feel like yourself again, and parent better for it.

options.text: Accept that the old you is just gone for good
options.consequence: Reclaiming small pieces brings you back; writing off the old you entirely deepens the loss and the depletion.

scenarios.debrief: Reclaim small pieces of your identity; the 'old you' isn't gone for good, and you parent better whole.

scenarios.hook: Match each small act to the need it meets.
scenarios.relearn: Small acts, a quiet chai, a friend's call, a little hobby time, meet real needs that keep a parent whole.

pairs.left: A call with an old friend

scenarios.hook: Sam: your child benefits from a parent who is also still a person. Feel the truth of that?
scenarios.relearn: Your child benefits from a parent who's also still a whole person.
scenarios.affirm: A child benefits from a parent who remains a whole person, not one who has erased themselves entirely.

scenarios.hook: You want to ask your partner to cover so you can take an hour for yourself, without guilt. You ask.
scenarios.relearn: Asking plainly and guilt-free for what you need makes it likelier to happen and models healthy needs.

yourLine.text: "I need an hour to myself today to recharge, can you take over? It'll help me be a better parent too."
"Sorry to ask, ignore me if it's too much, I'll manage somehow."

scenarios.hook: Spot what keeps a parent's own self alive.
scenarios.relearn: Keep your self alive by guarding a little time and staying connected to who you are.

scene.text: Guarding a little time of your own
Feeling you must be 'on' every hour
Staying connected to who you are

scenarios.why: Guarding a little time and staying connected to yourself keep you whole; being 'on' every hour erases you.

scenarios.hook: "A parent's only job is the child; their own happiness is irrelevant."
scenarios.relearn: Your happiness as a parent matters, both in itself and because it shapes the home your child grows up in.

myth.un: A parent's only job is the child; their own happiness is irrelevant.
myth.re: A parent's wellbeing shapes the home and the child; your happiness matters in its own right and for them.
myth.why: Happy parents help raise happy kids.

scenarios.hook: Relatives imply that wanting time or space makes you ungrateful for your child.
scenarios.relearn: You can adore your child and still have needs; don't suppress them to seem grateful.

options.text: Hold that loving your child and having needs both fit
options.consequence: You keep your needs without guilt.

options.text: Suppress your needs to seem grateful enough
options.consequence: Holding that love and needs coexist keeps you whole; suppressing needs to look grateful drives you toward burnout.

scenarios.debrief: Loving your child and having your own needs both fit; you don't have to suppress one to prove the other.

scenarios.hook: Sam: needing rest, help and a self doesn't make you less of a parent; it makes you a sustainable one. Agree?
scenarios.relearn: Needing rest, help and a self makes you a sustainable parent, not a worse one.
scenarios.affirm: Needing rest, help and a sense of self makes you a sustainable parent, not a lesser one.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to hold your identity as a parent, or one that erases you?
scenarios.relearn: Being both a devoted parent and your own person, with needs sometimes met, is healthy; total self-erasure isn't.

items.text: Both devoted parent and your own person

scenarios.hook: "Any sadness after birth is just weakness you should hide."

myth.un: Any sadness after birth is just weakness you should hide.
myth.re: Mild 'baby blues', tearfulness and mood swings in the first days, are very common and usually pass; they're not weakness.
myth.why: Early blues are a normal, passing wave.

scenarios.hook: "Postnatal depression isn't real; new mothers just need to cheer up."
scenarios.relearn: Postpartum depression and anxiety are real, common conditions needing care, not a 'cheer up'.

myth.un: Postnatal depression isn't real; new mothers just need to cheer up.
myth.re: Postpartum depression and anxiety are real, common medical conditions, affecting around one in five mothers in India, and they need care, not 'cheer up'.
myth.why: It's an illness, not an attitude.

myth.un: Only mothers get depressed after a baby; fathers are unaffected.
myth.re: Fathers can develop postnatal depression too, around one in ten, so partners should watch out for and support each other.

scenarios.hook: You notice your partner has seemed hopeless and withdrawn for weeks since the birth.

options.text: Say nothing and assume they'll snap out of it
options.consequence: Gently raising it and encouraging support helps; assuming they'll 'snap out of it' leaves a treatable illness unaddressed.

scenarios.debrief: If a partner seems hopeless and withdrawn for weeks after birth, gently raise it and encourage support together.

scenarios.hook: Sam: postnatal depression and anxiety are common and treatable; spotting them early changes everything. Hear that?
scenarios.relearn: Postnatal depression and anxiety are common and treatable; spotting them early changes everything.
scenarios.affirm: Postnatal depression and anxiety are common and treatable, and recognising them early makes recovery far more likely.

scenarios.hook: "Having a dark or scary thought as a new parent makes you a monster."

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help with parenting or your mood means you're a weak parent."

scenarios.hook: Sam: knowing the number before you need it is a quiet act of self-care. Worth saving them now?
scenarios.relearn: Knowing the helpline before you need it is a quiet, powerful act of self-care.
scenarios.affirm: Saving crisis and support numbers before you need them is a simple, powerful act of looking after yourself.

scenarios.hook: You're not sure your struggle is 'serious enough' to call a helpline or see a doctor.
scenarios.relearn: Reach out even if unsure it's 'serious enough'; you needn't be in crisis to deserve support.

options.text: Reach out anyway, you don't have to be in crisis to deserve support
options.consequence: You get help early, when it's easiest.

options.text: Talk yourself out of it until it's much worse
options.consequence: Reaching out while unsure gets help early; talking yourself out of it until it worsens makes recovery harder.

scenarios.debrief: You don't have to be 'serious enough' or in crisis to call for support; reaching out early is valid and wise.

scenarios.hook: Match a moment to the right India support.
scenarios.relearn: Tele-MANAS, KIRAN and a doctor are there for support, and emergency 112 for immediate danger.

scenarios.hook: Spot the sustainable way to look after yourself as a parent.
scenarios.relearn: Looking after yourself well is small daily care and early help, not ignoring yourself until you break.

scene.text: Small daily self-care and a support net
Ignoring yourself until you break
Reaching for help early and often

scenarios.why: Small daily self-care, a support net and early help are sustainable; ignoring yourself until you break isn't.

scenarios.hook: Sam: a well-looked-after parent is the foundation of a well-looked-after child. Feel the weight of that?
scenarios.relearn: A well-looked-after parent is the foundation of a well-looked-after child.
scenarios.affirm: Looking after yourself is foundational, not optional: a well parent is the ground a well child grows on.

scenarios.hook: "Once I'm coping a bit better, I can stop looking after myself again."
scenarios.relearn: Self-care is ongoing, not a one-off; keeping small habits and supports is what prevents sliding back.

myth.un: Once I'm coping a bit better, I can stop looking after myself again.
myth.re: Self-care is ongoing, not a one-time fix; keeping the small habits and supports is what stops you sliding back.

scenarios.hook: Your partner asks how you both can stay okay through the parenting years. You set the tone.
scenarios.relearn: A shared tone of honest check-ins, shared rest and openness to help keeps both parents okay through the long haul.

yourLine.text: "Let's check on each other honestly, take turns to rest, and never be too proud to get help."
"Let's just power through and hope for the best."

scenarios.hook: Your partner keeps insisting they're fine while clearly running on empty. You want to give them real permission to rest.
scenarios.relearn: Telling a depleted partner they don't have to earn rest, and covering for them, lets them actually refill.

yourLine.text: "You don't have to earn rest, take a break, I've got things, you matter too."
"Push through, you'll be fine, we all are."

scenarios.hook: Sort: refills a depleted parent, or drains them further?
scenarios.relearn: Naps, a night off and being cooked for refill you; saying yes to everything and skipping your own care drain you.

items.text: A nap or a shared night off

scenarios.hook: A relative implies you're a bad mother for wanting an evening out. You want to hold your ground gently.
scenarios.relearn: Naming that love and needs coexist holds your ground without guilt or a family fight.

yourLine.text: "Loving my child and needing a break both fit, this break helps me be a better parent."
"You're right, I shouldn't be so selfish."

scenarios.hook: Match each parent need to why honouring it helps the child too.
scenarios.relearn: Honouring rest, connection and identity makes you calmer, steadier and a fuller model, which helps your child.

pairs.right: A parent who models a full life

scenarios.hook: You think your partner may have postnatal depression and want to raise it with love, not alarm.
scenarios.relearn: A loving, non-alarming 'you're not alone, let's get support together' opens the door to help, not shame.

yourLine.text: "I've noticed how heavy things feel for you lately, you're not alone, can we get some support together?"
"Why can't you just be happy? We have a baby."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a caring, accurate response to a struggling new parent, or a harmful one?
scenarios.relearn: 'Common and treatable' and 'you're not alone' are caring; 'snap out of it' and 'good mothers don't' are harmful.

items.text: 'This is common and treatable, let's get help'

scenarios.hook: You finally decide to call a helpline but feel nervous about it. You picture how to start.
scenarios.relearn: A simple, honest opening is all a helpline needs; you don't have to have the words perfect to get support.

yourLine.text: "Hi, I'm a new parent and I've been really struggling, I wasn't sure who else to talk to."
"Sorry, never mind, it's probably nothing, I'll hang up."

scenarios.hook: Match each worry about reaching out to the reassuring truth.
scenarios.relearn: Each worry about reaching out has a reassurance: no judgement, no threshold needed, and support that helps.

pairs.right: Helplines and doctors are there to support, not judge
You don't have to be in crisis to call

scenarios.hook: Spot the strong, healthy move when you're struggling.
scenarios.relearn: The strong move when struggling is to tell someone and reach for support, not to hide it.

scene.text: Telling a trusted person
Hiding it to protect your image
Calling a doctor or helpline

scenarios.why: Telling someone and calling for support are strong, healthy moves; hiding to protect an image isn't.

scenarios.hook: A friend is coping with parenting stress in an unhealthy way. You want to steer them gently.
scenarios.relearn: A gentle, non-judging offer of a healthier alternative helps a friend far more than a harsh warning.

yourLine.text: "I get why you reach for that, want to try a walk or a chat with me instead next time?"
"You're going to ruin your life doing that."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a coping habit that helps in the long run, or one that costs you later?
scenarios.relearn: Talking it out and a daily wind-down help long-term; nightly numbing and no sleep cost you later.

items.text: Running on caffeine and no sleep

scenarios.hook: Match each hard feeling to a healthy first response.
scenarios.relearn: Overwhelm, isolation and wired exhaustion each have a gentle first response that steadies you.

pairs.right: Slow your breath, drop your shoulders
Rest your body even if sleep won't come

scenarios.hook: You want to set up your phone so help is one tap away on a bad day. You tell your partner the plan.
scenarios.relearn: Saving help contacts in advance means that on a bad day support is one tap away, not a frantic search.

yourLine.text: "Let's save Tele-MANAS, our doctor and a couple of people, so on a bad day help is one tap away."
"We'll look up numbers if we ever really need them."

scenarios.hook: Your partner asks how to know when it's time to actually get professional help. You answer warmly.
scenarios.relearn: A clear, warm threshold, lasting, heavier, or frightening, and sooner is okay, helps a partner act in time.

yourLine.text: "If it's lasting weeks, getting heavier, or scaring you, that's the time, and sooner is always okay."
"Only when you absolutely can't function at all."

scenarios.hook: Spot the response that treats a parent's mental health as it deserves.
scenarios.relearn: A parent's mental health deserves warmth and real resources, never 'it's nothing, move on'.

scene.text: Meeting struggle with warmth and resources
Telling them it's nothing, move on
Helping them reach real care

scenarios.why: Warmth-plus-resources and helping reach care treat mental health seriously; 'it's nothing' dismisses it.
